data_flow: Raw $_POST['value'] is only passed through stripslashes() and written with file_put_contents() to uploads/booking-package/front_end.js (line 6066) without sanitisation. That file is enqueued and served to every front-end visitor (index.php:1175, 3970), so script injected here runs on all pages.

The per-booking cancellationToken is hash('ripemd160', timeKey . scheduleUnixTime . microtime(true)), built only from public slot values and a microsecond clock reading, not from a CSPRNG. Anyone who can narrow the booking time can guess it and then retrieve full booking details (myBookingDetails) or cancel the booking via key plus token.

In selectedMode(), the 'refreshToken' branch passes the raw $_POST['key'] to Setting::refreshToken(). The method only applies sanitize_text_field() and then calls update_option($key, $token), so the caller chooses the name of any WordPress option to overwrite. The guard is only the Editor-level check (edit_others_posts or the plugin's editor/manager roles) in selectedMode(), with no allowlist on option names. The written value is a hash, so the attacker controls the option name rather than the value.

Anonymous POST sets mode, which registers getDownloadCSV on admin_init. Because DOING_AJAX is true, the capability gate at lines 5300-5302 is skipped. The only check left is wp_verify_nonce on $_POST['nonce'] with the 'download' action, and that nonce is printed to every visitor by localizeScript (index.php:5616, called from the front-end shortcode at 1484). Schedule::getDownloadCSV (lib/Schedule.php:7260-7291) then selects booked-customer rows by the attacker-supplied accountKey, month and year with no capability check, and the CSV is echoed at index.php:5326.

$_POST['key'] is passed to Setting::refreshToken (lib/Setting.php:2829), which sanitizes it only with sanitize_text_field and then calls update_option($key, $token) at line 2841 with a random hash value. The option name is fully attacker-controlled, so a privileged user can overwrite arbitrary WordPress options (for example users_can_register or default_role) with no allow-list. Gate is Editor-level, so 'admin' is used as the closest upper bound.

Unauthenticated GET unique is compared to wp_hash(get_site_url()) in Setting::updatePaidSubscription (lib/Setting.php:6744-6757), and the site URL is public, so the check does not authenticate the caller. A match triggers lookingForSubscription with stored IDs, which updates subscription state.

The shortcode front end emits nonce_download to every visitor (index.php:1484, localizeScript at index.php:5616); a POST to admin-ajax.php with that nonce passes the wp_verify_nonce check at index.php:5307 because the capability gate at 5300 is skipped under DOING_AJAX, and the request then runs Schedule.php:7260 getDownloadCSV, which reads $_POST parameters and has no capability check, and returns the booked-customers CSV.

$_POST['key'] (editor-level, nonce-protected) becomes the option name after sanitize_text_field at Setting.php:2831, and update_option($key, $token) at 2841 overwrites any wp_options entry with a generated hash, with no allowlist of permitted keys.

The 'orderby' request parameter is passed through sanitize_text_field (which does not escape quotes or parentheses) and, when it has no numeric field prefix so absint() yields 0, it is returned verbatim at line 2017. The result is concatenated into the ORDER BY clause in db_read_all() (class-ws-form-submit.php:400) without prepare or whitelisting. Access requires read_submission, which the administrator role holds.

The location POST value is accepted as the URL when its host matches the permalink host (1456-1484) and is assigned to options['url']. When the fetch returns an HTTP status of 400 or higher, get_url embeds $url unescaped in an href and in the link text (1018), and the message is echoed as HTML by save_as_pdf_pdfcrowd (1742, 1784).

The content-integrity token and date index are emitted in plaintext in the page's onclick (enc_data, lines 846-850, 862). validate_data derives its XOR key only from those public values (1436-1447) and accepts any payload that contains the token (1450), so an anonymous client can supply arbitrary HTML as cdata (1673) that is converted under the site's API credentials.

The remote response body fetched from a contributor-chosen url is inserted unescaped into the error message (wp_remote_retrieve_body at 1019 when the status is 400 or higher). The message is then echoed as HTML on the site origin to any visitor who clicks the button (1742, 1784).

The file name from get_output_name (1061-1086, which rawurldecodes the URL segment or uses output_name directly) is concatenated into $tmp_dir without sanitization (1517), and fopen with mode x creates the file at the resulting path (1518). The file is removed after the mail attempt, so the write is transient.

A contributor's shortcode attribute `file` (or data_file, page_watermark, client_certificate, attachments, conversion_config_file) is not filtered, so it is copied into custom_options and encrypted into the button's options blob. When any visitor POSTs that blob to the unauthenticated AJAX action, it is decrypted and merged into $options, prepare_conv (lines 1262-1268) places the path in $files, and build_body calls file_get_contents() on that arbitrary local path. The file contents are uploaded to the PDFCrowd API and the resulting PDF is returned to the visitor.

A `button_text` shortcode attribute is accepted by eval_shortcode (lines 943-949) without sanitization because it has the button_ prefix. get_button_text (lines 534-559) returns it unchanged, and create_button_from_style concatenates it raw into $button_content, which is output into the page HTML. The admin validate() escapes button_text with esc_html, but that path is bypassed for shortcode attributes.

When button_indicator_html is present, the sanitization branch for non-unfiltered authors runs wp_kses_post on $attrs['button_custom_html'] instead of $attrs['button_indicator_html'], so the indicator attribute stays unfiltered. Setting button_indicator="html" makes create_button_from_style (lines 733-737) emit that raw value into the public page.

Shortcode attributes such as button_custom_indicator, button_indicator, email_dialogs, email_recipient and email_custom_dialogs (lines 613-626, 699, 581) flow into $config, which is passed through json_encode without HTML-attribute escaping. The JSON is interpolated into an onclick attribute delimited by single quotes at line 713, so a single quote in the value closes the attribute and injects event handlers.

$_POST['location'] (same host as the blob's permalink) becomes $options['url'] and is fetched by get_url. On a status >= 400 response, the URL is interpolated unescaped into an href attribute and the remote response body is concatenated unescaped into the error HTML returned by get_error_page. A cross-site POST can therefore inject script into the admin-ajax response.

When the button's configured email_recipient is 'prompt', the recipient is taken directly from the unauthenticated $_POST['recipient'] with no validation or capability check. The address is then used as the To: of wp_mail (line 1592) with the generated PDF attached, so the site's mail system can be used to send to arbitrary addresses.

Unauthenticated $_POST['cdata'] is base64-decoded and XORed with a key built only from the public _token and date index (which the page exposes in enc_data). The only check is that the result contains the token string, which is trivially satisfied, so attacker-chosen HTML is accepted as $options['text'] (line 1673) and converted via the site's API credentials.

The restriction that strips custom_javascript and on_load_javascript for non-unfiltered_html authors only runs when button_custom_html or button_indicator_html is present in the attributes (line 916). A contributor can supply custom_javascript without either attribute, and it is carried into the conversion options that are sent to the remote converter.

The URL path segment from the attacker-supplied location (same host as the permalink) is split on '/' and then rawurldecode'd at line 1082, so %2F sequences become directory separators. The result becomes the attachment name, which make_temporary_file joins onto the upload temp directory (line 1517) to create and write a file outside it when email disposition is used.

A contributor sets the button_text shortcode attribute; eval_shortcode copies any button_* attribute into $options without sanitizing it (only button_custom_html/button_indicator_html get wp_kses_post, and only in one branch). get_button_text() returns button_text raw, and create_button_from_style() concatenates it into $button_content (lines 718-726) and the output HTML (line 740), so it is rendered unescaped to every visitor.

A contributor sets button_indicator=custom and button_custom_indicator to a string containing a single quote. That value is placed into $config['indicator'] (lines 619-623), serialized with json_encode (which does not escape single quotes) and embedded in the single-quoted onclick='...' attribute at line 713, so the quote breaks out of the attribute and injects script executed on click by visitors.

When the admin has set email recipient mode to 'prompt' and disposition to 'email', the unauthenticated POST parameter 'recipient' is returned as $options['email_to'] (line 1608, set at line 1718) and passed to wp_mail with the generated PDF attached (line 1592-1596), so any visitor can make the site send the PDF to an arbitrary address.

A contributor sets email_recipient_address (and email_cc, email_bcc, email_from) in shortcode attributes; these are trusted from the encrypted blob, used as $email_to (line 1560) and concatenated into the mail headers at lines 1584-1590 without validation, and wp_mail sends the server-generated PDF to that address, enabling arbitrary mail relay and header injection.

The request URL (derived from the attacker-supplied POST 'location', which only needs to match the site host) is interpolated without escaping into the HTML at line 1018 as href='$url' and as text, and the raw response body is also embedded at line 1019; the resulting WP_Error message is echoed as HTML by get_error_page() at line 1784 for non-email dispositions.

A contributor sets button_indicator="custom" and button_custom_indicator to a string containing a single quote; eval_shortcode stores it without restriction (lines 940-957). create_button_from_style then places it through json_encode (line 708) into the single-quoted onclick attribute (line 713) without esc_attr, so a quote breaks out of the attribute and injects an event handler.

The unauthenticated POST parameter $_POST['recipient'] is returned without validation (line 1608), assigned to $options['email_to'] (line 1718), and passed to wp_mail (line 1592). The site therefore sends a PDF and the attacker's chosen subject/content to any address, with no is_email check or rate limit.

The token-verification XOR key is derived entirely from values published in the page (the token and the day-of-year index in the enc_data JavaScript array, lines 849-850), so an attacker can craft cdata that passes the strpos check. The result is then used as $options['text'] (line 1673) and converted to a PDF, which lets an unauthenticated user inject arbitrary HTML into the converter.

The sanitization branch for a non-unfiltered author applies wp_kses_post to $attrs['button_custom_html'] twice, so the button_indicator_html attribute is never sanitized (line 931 writes the wrong key). It is copied to $options (line 949) and emitted raw into the page at line 737 when button_indicator is html, although wp_kses on post save partly limits the payload.

Contributor-authored shortcode attribute button_indicator_html (with button_indicator=html) -> eval_shortcode copies it into $options; the unfiltered_html sanitizer at 930-931 wrongly re-sanitizes button_custom_html instead of button_indicator_html, so the value is unfiltered -> create_button_from_style 736-737 echoes it raw into the page for every visitor.

Contributor-authored shortcode attribute file (also data_file, attachments, page_background, conversion_config_file, client_certificate) -> eval_shortcode stores it in encrypted custom_options -> save_as_pdf_pdfcrowd decrypts it (1636-1647) -> prepare_conv 1245-1268 places it in $files without path checks -> build_body 1107 file_get_contents() reads any server-readable path and uploads its content to api.pdfcrowd.com, with the result returned to the visitor who clicks the button.

Contributor-set shortcode attribute 'file' (or data_file, page_background, client_certificate, conversion_config_file, attachments) is merged into custom_options at eval_shortcode 940-957 and server-encrypted at 865-868; the visitor's nopriv AJAX request decrypts it at 1636-1646, prepare_conv 1266-1268 moves it to $files, and build_body 1107 calls file_get_contents() on it with no path restriction, so the local file's content is sent to the pdfcrowd API and returned in the PDF.

The args['status'] value is sanitized only with sanitize_text_field (line 1400) and passed to wp_update_post (line 1402). The handler checks only edit_post on the post, never publish_posts, so a contributor can move its own draft to publish or future status and bypass the publishing restriction. wp_schedule_post sets post_status 'future' at line 1457 with the same missing check.

Anchor href values are extracted from post_content with preg_match_all (line 5389). Each non-fragment, non-mailto/tel URL is passed unfiltered to wp_remote_head at line 5394, with no private-address or scheme restriction, and the response status or error is returned to the caller. Requires manage_options, so impact is limited to admins reaching internal hosts.

The only check is edit_post on the target post, which a contributor holds for their own drafts. The caller-supplied 'status' is passed through sanitize_text_field into wp_update_post() at line 1402 with no publish_posts check, so a contributor can set status to 'publish' and bypass the publish capability that the create path (line 1379) enforces.

Post meta is returned raw, either a single key or the full get_post_meta() array, gated only by read_post. Unlike wp_get_user_meta, no is_sensitive_key() or redact_sensitive_keys() filtering is applied, so credentials or tokens that third-party plugins store in post meta (on posts the caller can read) are returned in the JSON response.

A contributor stores an arbitrary non-underscore meta string on their own post via wp_update_post_meta (sanitize_text_field keeps serialized-looking strings); wp_duplicate_post reads it with get_post_meta and passes each value to maybe_unserialize() at line 1445, so a crafted serialized object is unserialized server-side, with exploitation depending on available gadget classes.

Attacker-supplied name, surname, profile fields and list selections from build_subscription() are merged into an existing CONFIRMED subscriber via merge_in() and saved with save_user(), with no proof of ownership of that email address. Depends on the if_exists configuration.

The `id` GET parameter is cast to int at line 238 and passed to get_email_field(), which reads the `message` column of any email with no status, private or draft check. The code then returns the substring between `<style>` and `</style>` as text/css at lines 249-251. Style blocks of unsent, draft or private newsletters are therefore readable without authentication.

The attacker-supplied $_REQUEST['redirect'] is passed through esc_url_raw() (line 196), and the only check is strpos($url, home_url()) !== 0 (line 200). That check is a string prefix match, so a host such as https://<site>.attacker.tld passes it, and wp_redirect() at line 207 (not wp_safe_redirect) sends the browser there. The request needs a valid subscriber key (nk), which an attacker can obtain by subscribing to the site, and an antibot check that only requires a POST with a fresh ts field.

$_REQUEST['redirect'] is passed through esc_url_raw() and then checked only with strpos($url, home_url()) !== 0, which accepts any host that merely starts with the site URL (e.g. the site URL followed by an attacker-controlled domain suffix). The value then reaches wp_redirect($url) at line 207.

$_GET['id'] is cast to int and passed to get_email_field($id,'message'). No status, private flag or capability check is applied, so the embedded <style> content of any email, including drafts, is echoed as text/css at line 251.

POST 'doc_type' is sanitized only with sanitize_text_field (line 4693) and concatenated into $doc_file_loc (line 4700). A RecursiveDirectoryIterator then walks that location and adds every .pdf or .html file it finds to a zip (lines 4709-4719), so files outside the plugin temp directory can be archived. The zip is then offered for download through download_temp_zip_file.

POST 'codeview_html' is passed to strip_unwanted_tags (customizer.php line 79), which only removes script, iframe, audio and video blocks by regex after html_entity_decode. Event-handler attributes and other active markup survive, and the result is saved to an option via set_preview_pdf_html (line 101) and later rendered in the preview.

Attacker-supplied base64 'post' (order ID) and 'email' parameters are decoded with wf_decode and the order is loaded with wc_get_order. Access is granted when the decoded email equals the order's billing email, with no secret or nonce required, and the order document is then rendered and sent to the requester via the wt_print_doc hook. Any wrong access_key falls through to this email-only check.

$_REQUEST['customizer_action'] is read at line 62 and used at line 63 in method_exists($this, ...) and $this->{$customizer_action}(). The $allowed_actions allowlist defined at line 61 (six methods) is never checked, so any method on the class is callable, including private and protected helpers such as delete_theme, activate_theme and save_default_template. The only gate is check_write_access() (login, nonce, manage_options or manage_woocommerce).

The GET file parameter is passed through sanitize_text_field, which keeps '../' sequences. The only check is that the name ends in '.zip'. The value is joined to the temp directory, file_exists is checked, and the file contents are streamed as an attachment, so any .zip file reachable by a traversal path can be downloaded.

POST doc_type (line 4802, only sanitize_text_field) -> delete_temp_files_recursively($doc_type) builds $backup_dir = get_temp_dir('path') . '/' . $doc_type (line 4842) with no traversal check -> RecursiveDirectoryIterator walks that directory and wp_delete_file() removes every .pdf/.zip/.html file found (lines 4845-4852). Guard is check_write_access (logged-in, _wpnonce, check_role_access), which does not constrain doc_type.
